thesis: Rudolf Kálmán's 1960 filter estimates something hidden, like a spacecraft's position, by blending predictions with noisy measurements and tracking its own uncertainty. It helped navigate Apollo to the Moon and now tells drones, robots and self-driving cars where they are.

story.title: Truth from noisy numbers
story.text: Rudolf Kálmán published a new way to estimate something that cannot be seen directly, such as a spacecraft's position, from measurements that are always a little wrong. That year he visited Stanley Schmidt at NASA Ames, and Schmidt's team adapted the filter for Apollo's navigation to the Moon.

story.title: Predict, then update
story.text: Each step, the filter predicts where the craft has moved using what it knows about its motion, and its uncertainty grows. Then a measurement arrives and the filter blends the two, trusting whichever is less uncertain, so the uncertainty shrinks. Repeated many times a second, a jagged track of readings becomes smooth and accurate.

story.title: How robots know where they are
story.text: Phones, drones, robots and self-driving cars run the same loop many times a second, fusing GPS, wheel sensors, cameras and lidar into one estimate. The filter is not machine learning itself, but the AI that plans a robot's next move depends on knowing where it is.

hint: Raise the measurement noise and the raw dots scatter wildly while the estimate stays close; turn the filter off to see what you would have without it.
